NFL Anytime Touchdown Scorer Odds: How They're Priced

Published September 23, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Open the props tab on a Sunday slate and you'll usually find a bell-cow running back sitting around -145 to score anytime, while that same player's team is -260 or shorter on the moneyline. New bettors often assume those two numbers should track each other, and end up either confused or convinced the prop is "off." It isn't off — it's answering a completely different question, built by a completely different pricing process, and the gap between the two numbers is actually one of the more useful things to understand about how prop markets work.

In this guide

  1. What "anytime touchdown scorer" actually covers
  2. Why a 20-player market prices nothing like a two-way line
  3. A worked example: the gap between moneyline and anytime-TD odds
  4. What actually moves a player's price during the week
  5. Mistakes bettors make with this market specifically

What "anytime touchdown scorer" actually covers

An anytime touchdown scorer bet wins if the named player scores a touchdown at any point in the game, by any method the sportsbook counts toward the market — rushing, receiving, and on many boards, a return or defensive score if that player happens to log one. It doesn't matter when it happens, whether the game is already decided, or what the final score ends up being. That's what separates it from the two tighter variants also on the board: first touchdown scorer, which only pays out for whoever opens the scoring, and last touchdown scorer, which only cares about the game's final six points. All three markets can carry very different prices on the exact same player in the exact same game, because they're measuring different things — full-game scoring share versus a single, mostly random sequencing event.

Why a 20-player market prices nothing like a two-way line

A point spread or a moneyline is, at most, a two-way market (three-way if you count the rare NFL tie separately, though most books settle that as a push). The implied probabilities of the available outcomes need to sum to roughly 100%, plus whatever vig the book is holding — usually somewhere in the neighborhood of 4-5% on a mainstream spread. An anytime touchdown board looks nothing like that. A single game might list fifteen to twenty-five players, from the starting backfield down to a third-string tight end who's drawn a plus matchup, plus sometimes a catch-all "any other player" or "no touchdown scorer" line.

Each of those individual prices carries its own embedded cushion for the book, and because touchdowns are a relatively scarce resource split across a lot of candidates, that cushion compounds fast. Add up the implied probability of every name on an anytime TD board and the total routinely runs well past 100% — often somewhere in the 15-20% range of aggregate hold, versus the mid-single digits you'd see pricing a spread. That's not a book being greedy for its own sake; a market this granular is harder to model precisely, thinner in total handle per outcome, and much harder for the book to hedge off to another operator, so the extra margin is the price of offering it at all.

A worked example: the gap between moneyline and anytime-TD odds

Say a team is -260 to win outright — using the standard formula for negative American odds, implied probability equals odds divided by (odds plus 100), so 260 / 360 works out to roughly 72%. Their lead running back, who's handling the bulk of the carries and most of the goal-line work, might sit at -145 to score anytime, which converts to 145 / 245, or about 59%. That's a real gap, and it's not a mispricing — it reflects how many different paths exist for that team to reach the end zone that don't involve this specific player.

A red-zone trip can end in a rushing touchdown for the lead back, but it can just as easily end in a short passing touchdown to a receiver or tight end, a field goal instead of a touchdown at all, a turnover, a quarterback sneak on a goal-to-go snap, or — in a lopsided game — work for the backup back once the outcome is no longer in doubt. A player can be the clear focal point of an offense and still miss the end zone in a meaningful share of his team's wins simply because touchdowns get distributed across a roster, not banked automatically to whoever touches the ball most. The anytime-TD price is the book's estimate of that specific player's share of a shared, limited resource — not a restatement of how likely his team is to win.

Takeaway: A star player's anytime-TD number and his team's moneyline are two separate models solving two separate problems. Don't use one as a sanity check for the other — use game script, red-zone role, and target share instead.

What actually moves a player's price during the week

A handful of factors move anytime-TD prices more than almost anything else, and none of them is simply "how good is this player":

  • Red-zone and goal-line role. A backup who only enters near the goal line can carry a shorter anytime-TD price than his snap count would suggest, because that specific role is where touchdowns actually get scored.
  • Team implied total. A team projected for 27-plus points offers more total scoring opportunities to divide among its players than a team projected for 17, which compresses prices across that entire offense even before matchup is considered.
  • Injury and role news. The moment a lead back or top target is ruled out, the next player up in the pecking order sees an immediate, often dramatic price move — frequently a bigger swing than that same news produces on the spread.
  • Opponent-specific matchup data. A defense that's given up an outsized share of touchdowns to a certain position or formation shows up in these prices well before it shows up in the point spread.

Mistakes bettors make with this market specifically

The most common error is treating a player's anytime-TD price as a proxy for how good or how heavily used he is, when it's really a proxy for how often he specifically finishes drives. A running back can lead the league in yards from scrimmage and still carry a longer anytime-TD price than a shorter-yardage teammate who happens to vulture goal-line work. The second common error is assuming first-TD-scorer and anytime-TD-scorer prices should move together — first-score pricing is heavily influenced by which unit gets the ball first and how the opening drive unfolds, which is close to a coin flip across a lot of candidates, so it behaves very differently from a full-game market. The third is not shopping the number: because these markets are priced with more individual judgment and less two-way balancing than a spread, the same player's anytime-TD price can vary by a wider margin from book to book than his team's spread ever would.

Frequently asked questions

Does a player's anytime-TD price include defensive or special-teams touchdowns?

It depends on the sportsbook's stated rules for that market — some boards count any touchdown the named player scores regardless of how, including a pick-six or a return, while others restrict the market to offensive touchdowns only. Always check the market rules on the specific book before assuming either way.

Why do backup running backs sometimes have shorter anytime-TD odds than their overall usage would suggest?

Because touchdown scoring is concentrated in specific situations, especially short-yardage and goal-line snaps. A backup who's specifically deployed in those spots can have a disproportionately high scoring rate relative to his total touches, which sportsbooks price accordingly.

Is it ever mathematically sound to bet a longshot anytime-TD price just because the payout is big?

Only if your own estimate of that player's scoring probability is meaningfully higher than what the price implies — the size of a potential payout says nothing about whether a bet offers value on its own. Compare the offered price against your own read of red-zone role and game script rather than chasing the largest number on the board.

Why does the same player's anytime-TD price vary more between sportsbooks than his team's point spread does?

Spreads get sharpened quickly by heavy two-way betting volume across the market, while a single player's touchdown prop carries far less handle and more of the book's own modeling judgment, so prices are slower to converge and can sit further apart from book to book.
